title: Small-Set Expansion Hypothesis
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
formal: For every rational constant \(\eta \in (0,1/2)\), is there a rational constant \(\delta \in (0,1/2)\) such that the following promise problem is NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions? Given a regular graph G on n vertices with \(\delta n\) an integer, distinguish YES: some \(S\subseteq V(G)\) with |\(S|=\delta n\) has \(\Phi _{G}(S)\le \eta\), from NO: every \(S\subseteq V(G)\) with |\(S|=\delta n\) has \(\Phi _{G}(S)\ge 1- \eta\).
why: A major proposed basis for hardness of graph partitioning and layout problems, with connections to Unique Games.

progress.text: Raghavendra–Steurer introduce the exact-size expansion promise and relate its hardness to Unique Games.
Raghavendra–Steurer–Tulsiani establish reductions and conditional hardness for Balanced Separator and Minimum Linear Arrangement.
A sparse least-squares lower bound is obtained assuming a randomized weighted exact-volume SSE variant.

definitions: Use finite simple undirected d-regular graphs \(G=([n],E), n\ge 2\) and \(d\ge 1\), given explicitly by their adjacency matrices. Regular means that every vertex has exactly d neighbours; d is not a fixed constant or an extra promise. For nonempty \(S, \partial _{G} S\) is the set of edges with exactly one endpoint in S, and \(\Phi _{G}(S)=|\partial _{G} S|/(d|S|)\). Internal edges contribute twice to d|S| and zero to the boundary. This is normalized edge expansion, not the number of outside neighbours. The graph has no promised connectivity, geometry or spectral gap. The constants \(\eta ,\delta\) are chosen before the input; they are not parameters tending to zero with n. For \(\delta =a/b\) in lowest terms, inputs have n a positive multiple of b, so exact set size has no rounding ambiguity. The YES and NO cases are disjoint since \(\eta <1/2\); inputs meeting neither case have no required decision answer. NP-hardness means that for every language L with polynomially checkable witnesses, a deterministic polynomial-time map sends each \(x\in \mathrm{L}\) to a YES graph and each \(x\notin \mathrm{L}\) to a NO graph. Equivalently, it suffices to supply such a reduction from Boolean satisfiability. Reduction constants and the polynomial exponent may depend on \(\eta\) and its chosen \(\delta\). The card fixes the unweighted regular-graph, exact-cardinality version of the imported question; weighted-volume, randomized-hardness and size-interval versions must be identified when cited.
answer_criterion: A positive resolution proves the stated NP-hardness for every \(\eta\) by choosing \(\delta\) and giving a valid promise-preserving reduction. A negative resolution refutes this quantified hardness statement for some fixed \(\eta\). Polynomial-time algorithms for every fixed \(\delta\) at that \(\eta\) would refute the hardness claim under \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\); an algorithm alone must not be called an unconditional disproof of NP-hardness. Results restricted to special graph classes or allowing a different output set size do not automatically settle this formulation.

context_blocks.title: What expansion measures
context_blocks.text: Choose a vertex uniformly from S, then choose one of its neighbours uniformly. The probability of leaving S is exactly \(\Phi _{G}(S)\). A set with expansion near zero is a group whose connections mostly remain inside it. Expansion near one means that almost every connection goes out. The promise asks whether one unusually insulated set exists at the specified size, or whether every set of that size is almost completely exposed.

context_blocks.title: Small means a fixed fraction
context_blocks.text: If \(\delta =1/1000\), the target has one thousand vertices in a million-vertex graph and one million vertices in a billion-vertex graph. Its size still grows linearly with n. Enumerating all sets of a fixed number of vertices therefore does not give a polynomial-time algorithm for the question. The order of constants also matters: \(\delta\) may depend on the desired expansion gap \(\eta\), and an algorithm for one convenient pair of constants would not refute the full hypothesis.

context_blocks.title: A sparse large cut can miss the issue
context_blocks.text: Take the disjoint union of two complete graphs on 50 vertices. Either whole component has expansion zero. Yet a two-vertex set contained in one component has expansion \(48/49\), and a two-vertex set split between the components has expansion one. Thus every set of the specified small size expands very well even though a larger zero-expansion cut exists. Optimizing over all sets up to half the graph can answer a different question from the exact small-size promise.

context_blocks.title: Why a large gap remains difficult
context_blocks.text: For a proposed set, its size and edge boundary are easy to count. The universal NO condition ranges over all sets of that size. The hypothesis asserts hardness even though YES and NO graphs are separated by a wide gap, with many intermediate graphs excluded by the promise. A graph expansion construction, a bound on one spectral parameter, or an algorithm with an uncontrolled change in set size is not automatically a distinguisher for this promise.

context_blocks.title: Connections and current boundary
context_blocks.text: Raghavendra and Steurer reduce small-set expansion to Unique Games, making this hypothesis a sufficient foundation for Unique Games hardness. Raghavendra, Steurer and Tulsiani relate it to a version of Unique Games with an additional expansion requirement and derive conditional hardness for graph partitioning and arrangement problems. This does not establish equivalence to unrestricted Unique Games in both directions. In August 2026, Lin, Mirrokni and Woodruff use a randomized, weighted, exact-volume variant to prove a sparse least-squares hardness result. Such an application assumes an SSE statement; it does not prove the statement itself, and its modeling conventions should not be silently transferred to this card. The checked sources leave the hypothesis unresolved.

sentences: Is it NP-hard to distinguish one poorly expanding small set from uniformly strong expansion at the same set size?
The target set occupies a fixed fraction \(\delta\) of the graph, with \(\delta\) chosen after the gap parameter \(\eta\).
Expansion is the fraction of incident edges that leave the set.
A sparse cut of a larger size does not necessarily reveal any poorly expanding set of the target size.
Known reductions connect the hypothesis to Unique Games and conditional hardness without resolving it.
